title: The flag and the wind
hookLine: two monks argue whether the flag or the wind moves; Huineng: your mind moves (Gateless Gate 29)

lines: A BANNER FLAPPING IN THE WIND.
THE ARGUMENT THAT ISN'T ABOUT THE THING.
cards: A temple courtyard in southern China. A banner flaps on a pole in the wind. Two monks stand under it, arguing, and getting louder.
It's like two people at dinner debating whether a movie was any good, and twenty minutes later the argument is clearly about something else entirely. Both are sure they're right.

Both are looking out, at the movie, at each other. Neither is looking at what's happening inside. A stranger is standing nearby, a lay worker from the south, and he's about to end the argument with one sentence.

teach.b: One monk says: the flag is moving. The other says: no, the wind is moving. Back and forth.
The stranger says: it isn't the wind moving, and it isn't the flag moving.
Your minds are moving. The two monks were struck silent.
The stranger was Huineng, remembered as the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, the Chinese school that became Zen.

The Platform Sutra, the book of his teachings, tells this as the moment he was recognized: a poor man from the south, by tradition unable to read, who had quietly received the robe and bowl of the Fifth Patriarch and had been hiding for years.
The Gateless Gate keeps it as case twenty-nine. Huineng isn't saying the flag is imaginary, or that wind doesn't exist. Each monk had grabbed one side and was defending it.
The movement that mattered was the grabbing: the mind flapping between flag and wind, mine and yours. Huineng turned their eyes around.
Then Wumen, in his comment, turns it once more: it isn't the wind, it isn't the flag, and it isn't the mind. In his verse, wind, flag and mind moving are all the same mistake.
Even your mind moves can become one more flag to argue about. The koan won't let you stand anywhere. What's left is just looking, before the arguing starts.
The Platform Sutra speaks of a mind that doesn't stick to anything. A flapping flag is a good place to look for it.

how: Zen communities honor Huineng as the Sixth Patriarch and study the Platform Sutra, which tells the flag-and-wind story; teachers use the koan to turn students' attention from outside arguments to the mind itself.

o: the Indian monk who first carried Zen to China
the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, a poor man from the south
a Chan emperor who built temples across the south

games.q: match each voice in the story.

s: Huineng says the flag is imaginary
he turns the monks' attention to their own grasping, not away from the world.
the Platform Sutra tells this as the moment Huineng was recognized
a poor man from the south who had received the Fifth Patriarch's robe.
Wumen's verse calls wind, flag and mind moving the same mistake
even 'mind moves' can become one more flag to argue about.

games.q: two monks under a flapping banner are arguing: flag or wind? they turn to you. you're Huineng. what do you say?
o: not the wind, not the flag: your minds are moving.
games.why: Huineng's answer silenced them, and Wumen later pushed further: not even the mind.

practice: Watch something that moves, a curtain, a leaf outside, the steam from a cup, or your own belly as you breathe, and notice how quickly the mind adds commentary: it's windy, I like that, I should close the window.
Each time, come back to just the movement. Then watch the mind itself moving, thought after thought, the same way, like a flag in the wind.

wordCard.voice: Huineng. The stranger who stopped two monks arguing about a flag and the wind by saying: your minds are moving.

orig.note: Chinese xīn dòng: the mind moves, the end of Huineng's answer.

carryVoice: Your line: mind moves. Not the flag, not the wind, but the grabbing. Day two hundred eighty-two.

sources.ref: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), case 29 and Wumen's comment and verse
